processing: In the village, leaves are briefly heated in a deep metal bowl over a stone hearth, kneaded in a rolling drum and dried on bamboo baskets. Most of the crop goes on to a factory in Phongsaly town.
harvest_season: February to May is the peak season. Prices fall in the rainy season from late May to October, and nothing grows from November to January.
appearance_dry: Large, dark, twisted leaves that lean brown from the village-style kneading.
appearance_liquor: Likely a clear yellow to light amber, as with other large-leaf rolled teas of the region.
appearance_wet: Large leaves in dull green turning brown.
taste_profile: Few reliable tasting notes exist; large-leaf tree teas of this region tend to be robust and slightly bitter with a lingering sweetness, and farmers say it lasts up to five steeps.

brewing.notes: Farmers say this leaf holds up for about five steeps, so brew it gongfu-style and start short.

vintage_note: Sold by season rather than vintage: the February to May picking is the prized one and fetches far more than rainy-season leaf. Most of the crop goes to China, often blended into other teas, so single-origin lots outside Laos are likely to be rare.
description:
Phongsali tea comes from old, tall tea trees in Laos' far north, best known around the village of Ban Komaen near Phongsaly town. The trees reach 4 to 10 metres, and that is what sets it apart from bush tea.

Processing is simple. At village level the leaves get a short heat in a metal bowl, a turn in a rolling drum, and drying on baskets; they start to brown along the way, so green is only a loose label here. Most of the crop goes to a factory in town instead.

Reliable tasting notes are scarce. Farmers claim about five steeps from a session against two for ordinary green tea, so treat it as a tea to brew short and repeatedly rather than one long mug.

Ask when it was picked: February to May is the season to pay for. The age claims need caution. The 400-year figure is widely repeated and rests on what villagers say.
history:
How old the trees are and whether they were planted are both open questions. Villagers say some are over 400 years old and believe they grew naturally, but nobody has dated them with certainty; reports speak of about 70 hectares in Ban Komaen and some 46,000 trees across the province.

The tea is tied to the Phunoy community. Today China is the main buyer, taking about two-thirds of what the town factory processes, frequently to improve lower-grade tea. Slow Food has listed it in its Ark of Taste as a tradition at risk, and the Swiss development group Helvetas has reported on these farmers and their tea.
